subject: Computer Networking
title: Multi-Factor Authentication
description: A short lesson to help you apply Multi-Factor Authentication.

hook.text: A hacker steals your password. They try to log in. A code pops up on your phone. They're blocked.

buildup.text: MFA requires two or more factors: something you know, something you have, or something you are.

discovery.text: Authenticator apps generate time-based codes. Hardware keys like YubiKey provide phishing-resistant proof of possession.

twist.text: SMS codes are better than nothing but vulnerable. SIM-swapping attacks redirect your texts to the attacker's phone.

climax.text: Google reported that hardware security keys eliminated phishing for all 85,000 of its employees. Zero incidents.

punchline.text: MFA means stealing a password isn't enough. Two locks beat one.

quiz.question: Why are hardware security keys considered the strongest MFA?
options: They are resistant to phishing attacks
They store your password in plain text
They work without an internet connection

details.summary: Multi-factor authentication requires two or more verification methods from different categories: something you know like a password, something you have like a phone or security key, and something you are like a fingerprint. MFA blocks over 99% of automated account compromise attacks.
details.whyItMatters: MFA is the single most effective defense against account takeover. Even if a password is stolen, the attacker cannot access the account without the second factor.
takeaways: MFA combines knowledge, possession, and biometric factors
Hardware security keys provide the strongest protection
MFA blocks over 99 percent of automated attacks

faq.question: What is the most secure form of MFA?
faq.answer: Hardware security keys using FIDO2/WebAuthn are the most secure because they resist phishing — they verify the website's identity before responding. TOTP apps are next best. SMS codes are the weakest MFA because they can be intercepted through SIM swapping. Any MFA is vastly better than none.

faq.question: Why don't more people use MFA?
faq.answer: Many users perceive MFA as inconvenient despite it adding only seconds to login. Organizations may not enforce it. Some older systems do not support it. User education about the overwhelming security benefit and simpler methods like push notifications are increasing adoption rates.
